segments.title: The Fog and the Law: Opening into Chancery's Maze

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, considered journey through one of the great novels in the English language.
Dickens published Bleak House in monthly parts between 1852 and 1853, and it has never quite released its grip on readers since.
It is a novel about fog — literal fog, legal fog, the fog that descends on a life when the Court of Chancery takes hold of it.
And it is a novel about everything else besides: love, secrets, class, disease, the will to survive, and the will to be good.
To help us unpack it, I have three exceptional guides with me today.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than any living performer — he hears the prose from the inside, and his delight in the language is utterly infectious.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished Dickens scholars of his generation — he reads Bleak House as a novel of moral character, and he will keep the rest of us honest.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who sees in Bleak House an anatomy of class power — the fog, for him, is never innocent.
We begin at the beginning — with Dickens's extraordinary opening, and with the world of Chancery that casts its shadow over every page that follows.
Oliver, you've read that opening aloud more times than most people have read it silently — what does it feel like from the inside?
It feels, every single time, like stepping into cold water.
The thing people forget about that opening is how funny it is — in the blackest possible way.
Dickens is not merely setting a scene — he is doing something to you rhythmically, hypnotically, before you've even realised it's happening.
And the same quality runs through a man like Tulkinghorn — who is perhaps the most perfectly written cold presence in Victorian fiction.
Dickens describes how Tulkinghorn moves between his London chambers and the Dedlock estate at Chesney Wold as though no distance separates them at all.
"He walks into Chesney Wold as if it were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he had never been out of Lincoln's Inn Fields."
No emotion, no fatigue, no sense of transition — he simply melts from one world into another.
That word — 'melts' — Dickens uses it twice in the same paragraph, and it is not an accident.
Tulkinghorn is not quite solid — he belongs to no world honestly, and that is what makes him so frightening to perform.
Oliver is absolutely right about the verbal precision — and I think it rewards examination in a moral key as well.
Tulkinghorn's impenetrability is not merely atmospheric dressing — it is a portrait of a man who has entirely subordinated his inner life to function.
He neither changes his dress before the journey nor talks of it afterwards — Dickens's syntax itself enacts the erasure of interiority.
Now, I want to place alongside that another portrait — Sir Leicester Dedlock at Chesney Wold — which I think illuminates something different.
Where Tulkinghorn is emptiness in motion, Sir Leicester is rootedness — almost geological rootedness — and Dickens renders it with extraordinary care.
He describes Chesney Wold as a place
"where the ivy and the moss have had time to mature, and the gnarled and warted elms and the umbrageous oaks stand deep in the fern and leaves of a hundred years."
That is not satire — or not only satire — that is a writer who genuinely feels the pull of such a place, even as he understands its politics.
Sir Leicester opposes the repose of Chesney Wold to what Dickens calls 'the restless flights of ironmasters' — and the irony, if it is irony, is considerably more complex than it first appears.
Edmund's reading is elegant, but I think it understates how precisely Dickens has mapped the ideology at work in that passage.
Sir Leicester is not merely rooted — he is invested, in every sense of that word.
The oaks and the ivy and the moss represent centuries of accumulated ownership — and Sir Leicester's comfort depends on no one questioning that ownership.
And look at what he does when confronted with the world beyond the park — he reads aloud from a newspaper to reassure himself.
Dickens gives us the scene precisely: Sir Leicester finds an article with what he calls 'congenial remarks bearing directly on the floodgates and the framework of society.'
"The man who wrote this article has a well-balanced mind," he announces — nodding at the fire, Dickens tells us, as if nodding down at the man from a mount.
That image — nodding down from a mount — is Dickens at his most surgical.
The well-balanced mind is one that agrees with Sir Leicester — and Sir Leicester's universe is arranged to ensure that such minds are the only ones he encounters.
Chancery, the aristocracy, the legal profession — they are all versions of the same closed circuit.
Daniel, that image of the closed circuit makes me think of something quite different — something almost farcical — which Dickens places right alongside all this grandeur.
Because the secrets that drive this novel — the hidden documents, the buried identities — don't just animate the powerful.
They drive the entire neighbourhood of Krook's rag and bottle shop into a collective delirium.
Dickens calls it, with magnificent grandeur,
"Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus' purse of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop."
A Fortunatus' purse — inexhaustible, magical, bottomless — applied to neighbourhood gossip about an old miser's rubbish.
And then the whole court imagines guineas pouring out of teapots, crown-pieces overflowing punch-bowls — the fantasy of hidden wealth runs like fever through every stratum of this society.
Even the pub singer — Miss M. Melvilleson, in the revived Caledonian melody — is in on it, angling her head toward the shop next door to comic applause.
It is ridiculous and it is wonderful — and it is entirely of a piece with everything else Dickens is doing.
Oliver has identified something I think is genuinely crucial — which is that Dickens democratises obsession.
The hunger for Krook's treasure is a comic mirror of the hunger that animates the great case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce itself.
Everyone in Bleak House is waiting for something that will never come — and everyone has convinced themselves that it will come, and soon.
That is not a critique of a system — that is a portrait of the human condition under certain kinds of institutional pressure.
The court of Chancery does not corrupt people — it reveals what people are prepared to become when hope is manipulated over decades.
I'd push back on that slightly — though not as far as Edmund might expect.
The court of Chancery doesn't just reveal character — it produces certain kinds of subjectivity.

The neighbours pouring over Krook's rubbish — they are not simply being human; they are being made into a particular kind of subject by a system that has taught them that the only route out of poverty is the miraculous windfall.
Dickens understands this even if he cannot quite theorise it — and that gap between his instinct and his analysis is what makes the novel endlessly fascinating.
He is more radical than he knows — and the text keeps escaping his intentions.
And that tension — between what Dickens intends and what the novel actually does — is something we'll be returning to throughout this series.
We've established the fog, we've met some of the figures who move through it — Tulkinghorn, Sir Leicester, the gossip-maddened neighbours of Krook's court.
In our next segment, we turn to Esther Summerson — the novel's other narrator, its moral centre, and one of Dickens's most debated creations.

segments.title: The Machinery of Ruin: Richard's Slow Dissolution

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time in the fog of Chancery, in the grandeur of Chesney Wold, in the humble warmth of Bleak House itself.
Today we turn to what I think is the novel's most quietly devastating story: the ruin of Richard Carstone.
With me are Oliver Trevelyan, who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps any living person and hears the music in every sentence.
Sir Edmund Leigh, who asks us to look at Richard's collapse not as social critique but as a study in moral character.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen, who sees in Richard's dissolution the workings of a system designed to consume young men exactly like him.
Let's begin with the diagnosis — or rather, the prognosis Esther herself offers early in the novel.
What Esther gives us in chapter seventeen is, in miniature, a theory of how systems reproduce their own failures.
She's describing an education that processes boys like interchangeable units — regardless of character, regardless of capacity.
And the result is a young man who has learned to dazzle rather than to endure.
Dickens puts it with that characteristic economy that looks simple until you read it twice.
"They were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters."
Servants become masters — that inversion is everything.
It's not that Richard lacks gifts — it's that his gifts have never been subordinated to anything larger than themselves.
The education system produced this, and then Chancery inherits the product.
And the fire-and-water figure is so right because it contains the danger already — you hear the thing about to go wrong even as you admire it.
Esther is one of those narrators who tells you the truth sideways — she says she liked him more and more even as she watches him dissolve.
There's a tenderness in her prose whenever Richard appears, even at the end.
What I find remarkable, reading it aloud, is that Dickens never lets Richard become merely pathetic.
He retains the gaiety and the quickness right to the very end — which is what makes the end so unbearable.
I think we ought to be careful not to externalize Richard's tragedy entirely.
Esther's observation is penetrating, yes — but it is an observation about character, about the weakness of a will that was never properly exercised.
Other boys passed through the same system and did not end as Richard ends.
Jarndyce sees this with terrible clarity, which is why his advice in chapter twenty-four is so unsparing.
"I ask you wholly to relinquish, for the present, any tie but your relationship."
Jarndyce is not being cruel — he is being honest about what Richard, left to his own course, will become.
He has seen it before, in Bleak House, as he says — and he knows the mechanism.
I won't entirely disagree with Edmund on Jarndyce — that is a moment of genuine moral weight.
But the mechanism Jarndyce has seen — what is it, exactly?
It is Chancery. And Chancery has a human instrument: Vholes.
Skimpole's speech about Richard in chapter thirty-seven is almost hallucinatory in the clarity of its satire.
He gives us this picture of Richard — sanguine, bursting with poetry — and his irony is devastating precisely because he is right and wrong simultaneously.
Right that Richard is young and bright and overleaping obstacles — wrong that this is sufficient reason to spare him the truth.
And so Richard falls into the hands of what Dickens shows us, through Vholes, is a perfectly legal system of slow consumption.
Skimpole is one of Dickens' great comic monsters — and the genius is that he's funny almost up to the moment he becomes monstrous.
That speech — 'sanguine, ardent, overleaping obstacles, bursting with poetry like a young bud' — it's nearly affectionate.
And then he simply washes his hands of the boy with a shrug of the most exquisite irresponsibility.
Dickens wrote Skimpole with Leigh Hunt in mind — and then spent years being mortified that everyone knew it.
But that particular guilt produced one of the finest comic performances in the novel.
The parallel I keep returning to is Tulkinghorn — not as a figure in Richard's story directly, but as its dark mirror.
Where Richard is all openness and expectation, Tulkinghorn is sealed — literally sealed.
Dickens gives us that extraordinary description of his rooms.
"Everything that can have a lock has got one; no key is visible."
That sentence is a portrait of a soul, not merely a room.
Tulkinghorn has achieved what Richard cannot: perfect self-enclosure, absolute control.
Yet the novel regards this as its own kind of damnation.
That's a striking juxtaposition, and I think it reveals something Dickens may not have entirely intended.
Tulkinghorn is the system's perfect agent — opaque, relentless, serving interests that are never fully named.
Richard is the system's perfect victim — bright, impulsive, delivered up to it by his own hope.
And between them sits Chancery — not a moral failing, but a machine.
I want to stay with Tulkinghorn a moment, because that passage is extraordinary to read aloud.
It begins almost as a description of the furniture — 'rusty, out of date, withdrawing from attention, able to afford it.'
"Rusty, out of date, withdrawing from attention, able to afford it."
And you realize that every adjective belongs to the man as much as the room.
That phrase — 'able to afford it' — is the one that stops me every time.
It's power described as detachment — the most chilling kind.
And compare that to Bucket — who is Dickens' other great legal figure in this novel, but so differently rendered.
Dickens gives us this marvellous image of him in chapter fifty-four.

"From the expression of his face he might be a famous whist-player for a large stake — say a hundred guineas certain — with the game in his hand, but with a high reputation involved in his playing his hand out to the last card in a masterly way."
Bucket has the same control as Tulkinghorn, the same mastery — but there is warmth in it, even compassion.
Dickens tells us there might be, 'but for the audacity of the idea,' a touch of compassion in Bucket's gaze at Sir Leicester.
What that parenthesis tells us about class — about who may feel compassion for whom — deserves an essay of its own.
Edmund is absolutely right about that parenthesis, and I'd go further.
'But for the audacity of the idea' — Dickens cannot quite let a working detective openly pity a baronet.
The class ceiling is even in the syntax.
And Sir Leicester, who 'remains immovable, with the same icy surface upon him' — he too is locked, like Tulkinghorn's furniture.
Only he reaches toward Bucket — the one man he trusts, and that man is a police inspector he would not have dined with a year before.
Richard never gets a Bucket — someone who is genuinely in his corner and competent enough to matter.
He gets Vholes, who is attentive, always attentive, in the way that a patient predator is attentive.
And he gets Skimpole, who watches him go under and calls it poetry.
The absence of a real friend — a capable, honest friend — is as structural to Richard's tragedy as Chancery itself.
Jarndyce tries to be that friend.
He tries, and Richard — out of pride, or perhaps wounded vanity — refuses him.
That is ultimately where I part company with Daniel's reading.
The system is villainous, yes — but Richard is also given the means of escape, in Jarndyce's advice and Ada's love, and he turns away from both.
Tragedy, in the old sense, requires an element of free choice.
And I'd say that the 'free choice' is itself produced by the system — that Chancery has so deformed Richard's sense of justice and entitlement that he cannot see clearly enough to choose well.
The promise of the suit — that something vast and rightful is owed to him — that promise was made before he was born.
He inherits not wealth but expectation — which is, in Dickens' moral economy, the most dangerous inheritance of all.
Expectation as inheritance — that's a thread that runs through half the novel, and it connects Richard to figures we might not immediately think to place beside him.
We'll follow that thread into the next segment, where we look at what Bleak House ultimately proposes as an alternative — if it proposes one at all.

segments.title: Secrets Behind the Veil: Lady Dedlock's Hidden Past

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the series in which we read Dickens' great fog-bound masterpiece closely, carefully, and with as much pleasure as possible.
Today we are deep inside the world of Chesney Wold — and the question at the heart of this segment is a deceptively simple one.
What does Lady Dedlock actually hide — and from whom?
With me today are three exceptional readers of this novel, each bringing a very different set of lenses to the text.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive — and he reads this novel first and foremost as a performer, alive to every rhythm and every joke.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford scholar who believes that Dickens' true subject is always individual character — its strengths, its failures, its moral weight.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as an anatomy of power — every relationship in the novel, for Daniel, is also a power relationship.

Oliver, let's begin with you — because the passage Dickens gives us on Lady Dedlock's place in fashionable society is one of the funniest things in the novel, and I suspect you've been waiting to get your hands on it.
I have been waiting — with indecent enthusiasm, I'll confess.
Because what Dickens does here is something only he could manage — he writes a passage of pure satire that is also, if you listen to it, a piece of music.
The whole argument rests on this wonderful, devastating inversion — Lady Dedlock believes herself utterly inscrutable, a creature beyond ordinary reckoning.
And Dickens says: every dim little star revolving about her knows her perfectly.
Her maid, her dressmaker, her librarian — they have all taken her exact moral measurements.
And then comes the image that I think is one of the great comic images in Victorian fiction.
"who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput."
Lady Dedlock and all her kind — reduced, in one brilliant sentence, to a fleet of tiny ships being dragged away by a man who pretends to bow before them.
What strikes me about that passage — and Oliver is right to relish the comic machinery — is that the comedy is doing serious analytical work.
Dickens is describing a system of class management — the way that tradespeople and service workers develop an expertise in the ruling class that the ruling class never develops about itself.
Lady Dedlock thinks she is sovereign — and she is, in legal and economic terms.
But she is also a product — catalogued, profiled, managed by those whose survival depends on knowing exactly what she wants before she knows it herself.
This is visible too in the housekeeper's room, when Mrs. Rouncewell offers her quiet, private verdict on her mistress.
Rosa is effusive — affable, graceful, beautiful, elegant — and Mrs. Rouncewell confirms all of it, with one precise reservation.
"Mrs. Rouncewell is not quite sure as to that... Mrs. Rouncewell thinks she would be more affable."
That ellipsis is everything — a pause in which decades of service and a lifetime of measured observation are contained.
Mrs. Rouncewell knows Lady Dedlock far better than Lady Dedlock suspects.
I take the point — though I would resist the framework of management and product, which seems to me to import rather modern categories into a Victorian novel.
What interests me in these passages is something older and more fundamental — the question of what it means to be truly known.
Lady Dedlock has constructed an identity — an immaculate social surface — and the novel's great drama is the progressive dissolution of that surface.
And no one in the novel understands the danger of that dissolution better than Tulkinghorn.
When he stands before her portrait and delivers his quiet, extraordinary verdict, Dickens gives us a line of almost surgical precision.
"A very good likeness in its way, but it wants force of character."
He is not speaking about paint on canvas.
He is naming the flaw he has identified in the woman herself — and he knows she knows it.
Edmund is absolutely right about Tulkinghorn — and the passage where Dickens introduces him at Chesney Wold is one I return to again and again as a performer.
There is a rhythm to his approach — never quickened, never slackened — that Dickens builds directly into the syntax.
You feel the man before you understand him.
And then comes that extraordinary sentence about what he carries with him — which I think you simply have to hear.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
And then Dickens turns to the question of motive — and delivers something genuinely chilling.
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret."
"He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself."
The man is a sealed vault — and the terrifying thing is we never entirely know what he values more: the secrets, or the power they give him.
Oliver's reading of Tulkinghorn crystallises something I want to push on — because the passage about Sir Leicester functions as a kind of diagnostic counterpoint to everything we've just said.
Sir Leicester is described as an excellent master — and Dickens is being entirely sincere about that, within the terms of his world.
But that excellence is built on a foundational act of erasure.
Dickens writes that he supposes all his dependants to be — and let me give you the exact words —
"utterly bereft of individual characters, intentions, or opinions."
He doesn't hate them — he simply cannot perceive them.
And yet — and this is the bitter irony Dickens plants in the paragraph — in extremis, it is Mrs. Rouncewell he trusts above anyone.
The person he has formally stripped of individual character is the one person whose individual character he relies on when he is most vulnerable.
That is a genuinely fine observation — and I'll concede it freely, because I think it illustrates something beyond class mechanics.
It illustrates the way that real character — moral seriousness, reliability, self-possession — has a force that cannot be entirely suppressed by social hierarchy.
Mrs. Rouncewell has it.
Lady Dedlock, for all her magnificence, is precisely what Tulkinghorn's verdict says she is — a likeness that wants force of character.
The secret she is hiding is not merely biographical — it is ontological.
Ontological — that is a word that will stay with me.

What we've been circling today is a kind of double exposure — the Lady Dedlock that society sees, and the woman behind that composed and beautiful surface who is being watched, known, and catalogued by nearly everyone around her.
Oliver, Edmund, Daniel — thank you for that.
In the next segment we will follow where that hidden past leads — and find Dickens at his most gothic and his most relentless.

segments.title: The Crossing-Sweeper's Testament: Class, Illness, and Invisibility

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great fog-bound novel seriously — which is to say, with deep pleasure as well as rigour.

Today's segment goes to the heart of the novel — the figure of Jo the crossing-sweeper, the institutions that grind him down, and the few stray acts of human kindness that mark his short, invisible life.
With me are three voices I trust completely on this material.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps anyone living — hears the rhythms of this novel as a performer first.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings a lifetime of Oxford scholarship and a conviction that the novel's moral imagination — not its politics — is where Dickens truly lives.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen reads every institution in this novel as a machine for protecting the powerful from the poor — and he makes that case with formidable precision.
Let's begin with the deathbed scene — Jo nursed by Phil Squod, visited by Jarndyce and Woodcourt, filling a small corner of a room with a weight entirely disproportionate to his station.
Oliver — you've read this passage aloud more times than most people have read it at all. What does it feel like from the inside?
The first thing that strikes you, reading it aloud, is Phil Squod — that extraordinary little figure with his smoky gunpowder visage and his one eyebrow.
Dickens gives him that single gesture — the nod, the raised eyebrow, "Hold up, my boy! Hold up!" — and it is the most tender thing in twenty pages.
Because Phil Squod is himself a grotesque — scarred, half-blind, lopsided — and here he is, this broken thing, nursing another broken thing.
Then Dickens steps back and gives us the line that haunts the whole passage.
"both thinking, much, how strangely fate has entangled this rough outcast in the web of very different lives."
That word — "entangled" — is doing everything.
It's not connection, not kinship — it's entanglement. Fate has caught them all in the same sticky thread without asking anyone's permission.
And the trooper — George — shedding "temporary vigour" upon Jo simply by standing in the doorway. That detail breaks my heart every single time.
Oliver puts his finger on precisely what distinguishes this passage from mere sentimentality.
The word "temporary" is doing its own quiet work, isn't it.
George's vigour is genuine, his sympathy is genuine — but it cannot be transferred. Jo cannot be saved by proximity to the healthy and the strong.
What Dickens is tracing here — and I think this is the moral centre of the novel, not the legal satire — is the testing of character under conditions of helplessness.
Jarndyce is there. Woodcourt is there. They cannot cure Jo. But they come.
That — the coming — is Dickens' idea of virtue. Not the achievement but the sustained effort of presence.
I want to hold onto Edmund's word — "helplessness" — because I think we need to ask who made that helplessness.
The individual virtue Dickens celebrates in that room — Phil's loyalty, George's warmth, Woodcourt's attendance — all of it is compensating for a structural failure the novel names very precisely.
Jo has been moved on, threatened, used, infected, and abandoned by every institution in the novel.
The web of "very different lives" Oliver read to us — those lives are not equally entangled. Jo is at the centre. The others pass through and return to safety.
And the mechanism that keeps Jo at the centre — that keeps him perpetually invisible and perpetually exposed — is something Dickens dissects elsewhere with extraordinary precision.
There's a passage in Chapter Thirty-Nine — the Vholes defence — where you can hear the whole apparatus of institutional self-protection speaking in its own voice.
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
And there it is — the system defending itself not in the language of power but in the language of respectability.
Vholes must be preserved because Vholes is respectable. And the law must be preserved because Vholes depends on it. It is circularity as political philosophy.
The Vholes passage is a masterpiece of comic ventriloquism, and Daniel is absolutely right about what it's doing — but I want to dwell on the pleasure of it for a moment.

Kenge's voice there is so perfectly self-congratulatory — that rolling, ceremonious rhetoric — "Diligent, persevering, steady, acute in business" — delivered as though he were describing St. Francis of Assisi.
And then the parliamentary minutes — the question numbers alone are the joke. "Question number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine."
Dickens is telling you: the machinery of inquiry has been running so long it has lost all contact with the thing it was supposed to inquire into.
The answer that ends the inquiry — "Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man" — that capitalised MOST is Dickens screaming through the page.
Which is his method — he makes you laugh, and while you're laughing, he puts the knife in.
I don't dispute the satirical force of that passage — it would take extraordinary wilfulness to dispute it.
But I notice that Dickens keeps his most sustained examination of institutional corruption separate from his most moving portrayal of individual failure.
Skimpole — who is really the more damaging figure in Jo's story — is not a lawyer. He is a man who has cultivated irresponsibility into an aesthetic.
Esther gives us the passage I find most chilling in all of Bleak House.

"what Harold Skimpole was, Harold Skimpole had found himself, to his considerable surprise, when he first made his own acquaintance; he had accepted himself with all his failings and had thought it sound philosophy to make the best of the bargain."
The phrase "sound philosophy" is the dagger. Skimpole has turned moral laziness into a philosophical position — and done so with considerable charm.
Daniel and I disagree about where the weight of the novel falls. But I think we agree that Skimpole is a monster — simply a monster made of silk rather than iron.
Edmund is right about Skimpole, and it's worth saying that Dickens was unusually brave in creating him.
The character was recognisably based on Leigh Hunt — Dickens' own circle — and Dickens wrote him without mercy anyway.
But what I'd add is that Skimpole's personal philosophy is also a class philosophy — and the novel makes that plain when he turns up at Chesney Wold.
He flatters Sir Leicester with a line about aristocratic patronage that is almost too perfectly observed.
"The owners of such places as Chesney Wold are public benefactors. They are good enough to maintain a number of delightful objects for the admiration and pleasure of us poor men."
"Us poor men" — from a man who will sell Jo to Bucket for five pounds without a second thought.
This is the ideology that makes Jo invisible: the aestheticisation of inequality, dressed up as gratitude.
Skimpole doesn't just fail Jo. He provides the cultural cover that makes that failure seem natural — even charming.
And then there's Tulkinghorn — the other great figure of institutional menace — who Dickens draws so differently from Skimpole it's almost as if he's demonstrating his full range of technique.
Where Skimpole is all warmth and surface, Tulkinghorn is — listen to this description.
"In manner, close and dry. In voice, husky and low. In face, watchful behind a blind."
Three parallel clauses, each one shorter than you expect, each one closing off another avenue of approach. The prose enacts the man.
And then Dickens slips in this wonderful ironic knife-twist at the end of the paragraph.
"The peerage may have warmer worshippers and faithfuller believers than Mr. Tulkinghorn, after all, if everything were known."
"If everything were known" — there's the whole novel in four words. The entire plot turns on what is hidden and what is known.
Tulkinghorn is the novel's great keeper of secrets — and unlike Skimpole, he knows exactly what he is and what he does, and does it anyway.
And Tulkinghorn is a reminder that Dickens — for all the social machinery around him — remains a novelist of character before he is a novelist of system.
We remember Tulkinghorn not because he represents the legal profession but because he is frightening in himself — particular, opaque, implacable.
Daniel will tell me the two are inseparable — the character and the system — and I shall concede a good deal of ground there.
But Dickens earns his indignation through portraiture, not through argument. That is his method, and it seems to me his genius.
I will take that concession gracefully.
But I want to end where we began — with Jo. Because I think what makes this novel extraordinary is that Jo's invisibility is not incidental. It is the thesis.
Skimpole flourishes. Tulkinghorn operates. Vholes persists. And Jo — who has done nothing wrong, who has only ever been "moved on" — dies in a borrowed room.
The novel asks us to feel that as an obscenity. And it asks us to ask — who made it so.
Jo's death — which we'll come to directly in our next segment — may be the most politically charged moment of grief in all of Victorian fiction.
Oliver, Edmund, Daniel — thank you. The web is very wide, and very sticky, and we've only begun to feel its extent.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Entanglement and Complicity: How Dickens Weaves the Web

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked — the podcast that takes Dickens' great fog-bound novel apart, page by page, passage by passage.
Today's segment is about complicity — about how this novel entangles people with one another, and with systems larger than themselves.
With us, as ever, are our three guides to the world of Bleak House.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man whose voice has brought more Dickens to life than perhaps anyone alive.
Oliver brings a performer's instinct for what makes a character tick on the page and in the ear.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, moral critic, and the man most likely to quote Burke when the rest of us are quoting Dickens.
Edmund reads Bleak House as a novel about character, conscience, and what people do with their freedom.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen — cultural historian, whose Bleak House is an anatomy of power — every institution a machine for protecting those who already have everything.
Daniel sees the entanglement of this novel in structural terms — and he earns every word of his anger with evidence.
Let's begin with a character who is the very image of charming self-exemption — Harold Skimpole.
Oliver, Skimpole is yours — and I suspect you've had some very particular thoughts about performing him.
Skimpole is one of the great comic monsters of English fiction — and I mean monster in the most affectionate possible way.
He is a man who has constructed an entire philosophical system to avoid paying his debts.
And the astonishing thing — the thing that makes him so difficult to perform — is that he does it with genuine charm.
Esther notices exactly this, and Dickens gives her a sentence that I find almost impossible to rush through.

"If I felt at all confused at that early time in endeavouring to reconcile anything he said with anything I had thought about the duties and accountabilities of life... I was confused by not exactly understanding why he was free of them."
That construction — "I was confused by not exactly understanding why he was free of them" — is a masterpiece of delayed bewilderment.
Esther knows something is wrong but cannot quite locate the wrongness — and that confusion is precisely what Skimpole relies upon.
On the page, that last line — "That he WAS free of them, I scarcely doubted; he was so very clear about it himself" — Dickens even italicises the WAS.
It's a stage direction buried in a novel.
Oliver puts his finger on something I think is quite crucial — the question of Esther's bewilderment.
Esther is, throughout this novel, the moral register — the person through whom we feel where genuine virtue lies.
And what Dickens tells us through Esther's confusion is not that Skimpole is a product of some systemic failure.
He tells us that Skimpole is a study in a particular failure of character — in the willful abdication of moral responsibility.
Burke wrote that society is a contract between the living, the dead, and those yet to be born — a chain of obligation.
Skimpole is Dickens' comic image of what it looks like when a man simply steps out of that chain entirely — and smiles while doing so.
I want to agree with Edmund on Skimpole's individual culpability — and then push a little further.
Because what makes Skimpole so devastating a creation is that he is not simply an eccentric — he is a parasite with a theory of parasitism.
He has aestheticised his own exploitation of others — turned it into a philosophy, a charm offensive, an art form.
And Dickens knew people like this — he based Skimpole on Leigh Hunt, and was apparently never quite forgiven for it.
But the structural point is this: Skimpole is only possible because a certain class of society agrees to excuse him.
The system protects him precisely the way Chancery protects Jarndyce — through a fog of social deference and aesthetic appreciation.
Daniel's word — aestheticised — is exactly right, and it connects Skimpole to something Dickens does throughout this novel with his comic grotesques.
They are all, in their different ways, people who have made a performance out of avoiding the claims of others.
Now Boythorn is the opposite case — a man whose performance is all surface violence and whose core is entirely warm.
Jarndyce sets him up with the most glorious deadpan in the novel.

"You must not be surprised to see him take me under his protection, for he has never forgotten that I was a low boy at school and that our friendship began in his knocking two of my head tyrant's teeth out — he says six — before breakfast."
"He says six" — tucked in those parentheses — that is Dickens at the height of his comic craft.
The disparity between two teeth and six is funnier than any punch line you could write — and Jarndyce tells it on himself with complete serenity.
The Boythorn passage illuminates something about Jarndyce's character that I think is rather important to the larger argument of the novel.
Jarndyce is a man who tells the story of his own humiliation — his status as a "low boy" — with warmth rather than resentment.
He values Boythorn's loyalty precisely because it was given without condition, without benefit — and he has carried it across a lifetime.
This is the novel's image of what genuine friendship looks like — and it is the standard against which Richard Carstone's collapse must be measured.
Which brings us, I think, to the most painful passage in this segment.
Richard Carstone is the novel's great study in what Chancery actually does to a person — not merely impoverishes them, but unravels their entire capacity for judgment.
And the cruelty is that it happens in the presence of Vholes — the most professionally hollow man in the novel — who simply lets Richard talk.
Listen to what Richard actually says.

"He becomes to me the embodiment of the suit; that in place of its being an abstraction, it is John Jarndyce; that the more I suffer, the more indignant I am with him; that every new delay and every new disappointment is only a new injury from John Jarndyce's hand."
The abstraction has become a person — and the person who has been most kind to Richard has become the abstraction's face.
That is what the system does — it doesn't just consume wealth, it consumes the capacity to perceive clearly who your friends are.
Chancery does not merely ruin Richard financially — it perverts his moral vision.
And standing over that speech, of course, is Vholes — who says almost nothing, and whose silence is perfectly designed to encourage Richard to go on.
When I've read Vholes aloud, I make him very still — very quiet — because everything he does is directed at keeping Richard talking, and spending.
It's the most chilling performance in the novel — because it has no performance in it at all.
I would resist, gently, Daniel's reading of this as purely systemic.
Richard is not simply a victim of Chancery — he is also a young man who will not be told.
Jarndyce tells him, with complete clarity, that the suit will destroy him — and Richard chooses, at each stage, not to hear it.
The system is corrupt — that much Dickens makes abundantly plain.
But Richard's tragedy is also a tragedy of character — of a weak will that mistakes obsession for principle.
I don't dismiss the weakness of will — but I'd ask what the system is designed to do with weak wills.
Chancery is not an impartial arena that randomly destroys whoever wanders in — it is constructed to consume exactly the kind of hope Richard has.
And then there is the counterpoint — Jarndyce himself, asking Esther when they shall give Bleak House its mistress.
"When shall we give Bleak House its mistress, little woman?"
Jarndyce is asking Esther to marry him — with such tenderness that it almost obscures the transaction.
A guardian, proposing to a ward he has shaped since childhood — the web of obligation and affection in this novel is never simple, even at its most tender.
That phrase — "little woman" — Dickens uses it so often for Esther that it begins to feel like a kind of gentle diminishment dressed as endearment.
And yet Jarndyce says it here so openly, so un-selfconsciously, that you cannot quite convict him of condescension.
He genuinely loves Esther — that is never in doubt.
But when I read this passage aloud, I always hear the structure of the sentence — "When shall we give Bleak House its mistress?" — and I think: who is that question actually for?
That is a perceptive observation — but I think we must resist reading Jarndyce's proposal as anything other than generous.
He is, after all, a man who will later release Esther entirely — who gives up his claim without bitterness or reproach.
In a novel full of people who take — Vholes, Skimpole, Chancery itself — Jarndyce is the great counter-example: the man who gives.
And this moment of happy anticipation — his delight here, his eagerness — makes his later sacrifice all the more quietly devastating.
We have the web, then — Skimpole who refuses obligation, Richard who cannot see past his obsession, and Jarndyce who is bound to others by something close to saintly generosity.
And Dickens puts them all in the same novel, breathing the same fog — which is itself perhaps the point.
In our next segment we'll move deeper into the machinery of Chancery itself — and ask whether Dickens believed it could ever be reformed, or whether he thought it had to be endured.

segments.title: Comic Relief and Moral Witness: Humor in the House of Sorrow

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens seriously — and joyfully.
Today we're turning to something that sits at the very heart of this novel's genius: its comedy.
Bleak House is, among other things, one of the funniest books in English literature.
But the laughter in Dickens is never innocent — it always has moral weight, social edge, or gothic shadow.
With me today are three people who know this novel intimately, each from a very different angle.
Oliver Trevelyan has read more Dickens aloud than any living person — and he understands better than anyone how the comedy lives in the rhythms of the prose.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings a lifetime of Oxford scholarship and a deep conviction that Dickens' moral imagination is finally what matters most.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen reads the laughter as something sharper — a dissection of class and power that Dickens could only make bearable by making it funny.
Let's begin with Oliver — and with one of the novel's most deliciously unsettling comic figures: the rag-and-bottle man, Krook.
Krook is one of those creations where you feel Dickens simply could not contain himself.
Here is this ancient, dusty, half-deranged rag merchant who keeps cats and lives in organised chaos — and Dickens gives him the gift of mystery.
The scene where Esther watches him produce these letters — forming 'Jarndyce,' forming 'Bleak House' — out of nowhere, for no apparent reason, is wonderfully sinister.
And then listen to what Dickens does at the end of the passage.
Three words: "he laughed again."
That's it. That's the whole effect.
Dickens doesn't explain the laugh, doesn't describe it, doesn't colour it with an adverb.
He just lets it hang in the room — and suddenly the comedy has become something altogether more chilling.
Oliver is quite right to dwell on the restraint there.
What strikes me about Krook — and about the comedy of this novel more broadly — is that it is always in the service of character.
The laugh tells us something essential about Krook that no amount of description could achieve.
He knows something. He will not say it. And he finds that power amusing.
That is a rather profound comic observation about human nature — and Dickens delivers it in three words.
I'd push that a step further.
What Krook actually represents in this novel is the underside of the archive — all the documents, all the accumulated paper of Chancery, reduced to rags and bottles.
His shop is a mirror image of the Court of Chancery itself — chaotic, hoarding, illegible.
So when Krook produces these names — Jarndyce, Bleak House — out of his chaos and then simply laughs, what we're seeing is the system mocking those caught in it.
The joke, such as it is, is on Esther — and on everyone Jarndyce has damaged.
I love that reading — though I think Dickens also simply loved writing Krook because Krook is tremendous fun to perform.
There's a theatrical tradition — going back to the readings Dickens gave himself — of playing the grotesques with enormous physical energy.
The comedy and the menace are not opposites in Dickens — they live in the same body, the same laugh.
From the gothic comedy of Krook's rag shop, let's move to perhaps the most purely comic figure in the novel — and Edmund, I think you've been waiting for this one.
Sir Leicester Dedlock: baronet, patriarch, and one of the great comic monuments of Victorian fiction.
Sir Leicester is a figure I confess to regarding with a great deal of affection — which is not, I suspect, how he is most commonly taught.
Dickens satirises him, certainly — but the satire is full of something very close to respect.
Consider the introduction Dickens gives him, and observe just how precisely the comedy is calibrated.
"He has a general opinion that the world might get on without hills but would be done up without Dedlocks."
The joke is perfect because it is exactly the kind of opinion Sir Leicester would hold — and he would hold it with complete sincerity.
And then Dickens closes the paragraph with what I regard as one of the finest comic sentences he ever wrote.
"He is an honourable, obstinate, truthful, high-spirited, intensely prejudiced, perfectly unreasonable man."
Each adjective earns its place — and then the last two detonate the whole edifice with magnificent comic precision.
That list of adjectives is absolute heaven to read aloud.
You build the rhythm — honourable, obstinate, truthful — and then Dickens pulls the rug with "intensely prejudiced" and lands the final blow with "perfectly unreasonable."
It's the structure of a joke that is also a character study that is also a verdict on a class.
All of that, in one sentence.
And we shouldn't mistake the warmth of that comedy for endorsement.
Dickens is doing something precise in the passage about Sir Leicester's house and his pictures — describing an art collection that is, frankly, rubbish.
"Miss Jogg the model" appears twice — once as Othello, once as a Spanish lady.
It is very funny. But what it shows is that the wealth and taste of the ruling class is built on recycled costume and pretension.
The comedy is the critique — there is no gap between them.
I wouldn't dispute the critique — but I think Daniel rather undersells what Dickens does with Sir Leicester by the end of the novel.
The same man — obstinate, perfectly unreasonable — is also capable of a loyalty to Lady Dedlock that is genuinely moving.
Dickens never makes him simply a target.
That, I would argue, is the sign of a moral imagination at work — not merely a satirical one.
And nowhere is that tension between comedy and something more tender more perfectly illustrated than in the Skimpole scene.
Because here we have Sir Leicester — the perfectly unreasonable man — in a scene that is simply a sustained exercise in magnificent comic indignation.
Sir Leicester cannot quite manage Harold Skimpole's name — and this matters enormously.
"Mr. Hirrold — Herald — Harold — Skampling — Skumpling — I beg your pardon — Skimpole."
That is Dickens performing a very particular kind of aristocratic comedy — the man so grand he cannot be expected to master the names of those below him.
But the joke is also on Skimpole — because to be nameless in Sir Leicester's world is to be perfectly invisible.
There is a further layer of comedy that one mustn't miss.
Sir Leicester's grievance — delivered with such gravity and such pain — is that this unnamed gentleman could not examine his pictures with sufficient leisure.
He reads it from a card. Through his eyeglass. Gravely.
And the card, we are led to understand, concerns the man whose irresponsible charm will eventually contribute to genuine harm in this novel.
The comedy here is entirely in the gap between Sir Leicester's magnificent solemnity and the utter triviality of his complaint.
Dickens understood that pomposity is funnier the more sincere it is.
The full quote is worth hearing in that light.

"I assure you, sir, it has given — me — pain — to learn from the housekeeper at Chesney Wold that a gentleman... was likewise deterred by some such cause from examining the family pictures with that leisure, that attention, that care, which he might have desired to bestow upon them."
Those dashes — "given — me — pain" — are the whole performance in miniature.
Sir Leicester is staging his own suffering as a public occasion.
And what he is suffering over is the fact that a sponger could not properly admire his inherited possessions.
That is a precise image of what the aristocracy actually is in this novel — a machine for generating the performance of wounded dignity.

And yet — and I want to come back to Edmund's point about the end of the novel — that same capacity for performance, that same depth of feeling about what is proper and honourable, is what makes Sir Leicester's love for Lady Dedlock genuinely affecting.
Dickens knew that the most moving things are often built on what we have previously been invited to laugh at.
The comedy is not a preparation for the seriousness. They are the same thing.
That feels like exactly the right place to pause — with comedy and seriousness declared inseparable.
We've seen Krook laugh his mysterious, knowing laugh; Sir Leicester sustain his perfectly unreasonable dignity; and Dickens use all of it to tell us something true about the world the novel inhabits.
In our next segment, we'll turn to what lies beneath that laughter — the figures the comedy cannot reach, and what the novel asks us to feel when it stops being funny.

segments.title: The Reckoning: Bleak House and the Persistence of Injustice

utterances.text: We've spent this episode inside the fog — legal, moral, and atmospheric.
Now, as we close, I want to ask each of you: what does Bleak House leave us with?
Not just as a literary achievement — though it is towering — but as a reckoning.
Edmund, let's begin with you.
What strikes me, returning to this novel for the fortieth or fiftieth time, is the precision of its desolation.
Dickens does not deal in vague grievance.
He gives us a specific street, specific houses, specific decay.
There is a passage where Jarndyce describes property that belongs, in name, to the suit.

"It is a street of perishing blind houses, with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door — and every door might be death's door — turning stagnant green."
Every door might be death's door.
That parenthesis is not rhetoric — it is the quiet moral truth of the whole book.
This is what unchecked institutional power produces: not merely inconvenience or injustice — but ruin, and death.
And what a sentence to have to read aloud.
It doesn't end — it accumulates.
Each clause adds another wound to the thing: no glass, no frame, no hinges, rust, sinking chimneys, green steps.
Dickens wrote that to be spoken, not read.
You feel it in the lungs — this long, failing exhalation.
And then Jarndyce says — with that terrible quietness — "these are the Great Seal's impressions, my dear, all over England."
The children know them.
The children know them — as if desolation were simply part of their education.
Edmund called it the product of unchecked institutional power.
I'd press that further: it's the product of a system that legally protects its own waste.
Notice what Jarndyce says — this is the property of costs.
"I ought to call it the property of costs, for costs is the only power on earth that will ever get anything out of it now."
The law has consumed the thing it was meant to adjudicate.
Those houses do not fall to ruin through neglect alone — they are held in a legal vice that prevents anyone from rescuing them.
That is not inefficiency.
That is the system working precisely as designed — to protect costs, not people.
I grant Daniel's point about the mechanism.
But I resist the conclusion that this is therefore a novel with a political programme.
Dickens does not offer us a remedy.
He offers us Bleak House itself — that extraordinary, eccentric, warm, imperfect home that Jarndyce makes for others.
Esther remembers it in terms that are almost unbearably tender, you know.
"With its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw."
That is the counter-world the novel imagines.
Not a reformed Chancery — but a better human being, who builds a better house.
That description of Bleak House in the early chapters is one of the great welcoming passages in all of Dickens.
The portraits that don't match, the rose-leaves in every drawer, the angels taking the complacent gentleman to heaven with some difficulty.
That last detail always gets a laugh when I read it — and it should.
Dickens earns the warmth of that house against everything the novel puts in its path.
All those perishing blind houses with their eyes stoned out — and then Esther's room with the oval engravings of the months.
That contrast is the novel's heartbeat.
I won't deny the warmth of that house, or the beauty of that writing.
But I think Edmund's reading, for all its generosity, is finally a consolation.
One good man builds one good house — while the street of blind houses stretches across all of England.
Dickens knows this.
The most damning line in the whole passage isn't the decay — it's the seal.
"These are the Great Seal's impressions, my dear, all over England."
The institution has stamped its mark on the landscape of the entire country.
No individual virtue — however genuine — can unstamp that.
I take that point seriously — more seriously, I think, than Daniel expects me to.
The novel does not offer a political solution because Dickens, I believe, had ceased to trust in them.
What remains is the human scale: what one person does for another.
Burke said something that applies here: "To love the little platoon we belong to in society is the first link in the series by which we proceed towards a love to our country and to mankind."
Bleak House is Jarndyce's little platoon.
Burke in the closing segment — Edmund, you never disappoint.
But I think what we're all circling is the same thing Dickens was circling, which is this: the novel holds both truths simultaneously.
The Great Seal's impressions are all over England — yes.
And there is light and warmth and the hospitable jingle of preparations for dinner — yes.
That is why we return to it.
Not for answers, but because it holds the weight of the question without flinching.
I think that may be the finest summary of Bleak House's achievement I've heard — and I've heard a few.
A novel that holds the full weight of its world's injustice, and still — improbably, stubbornly — keeps the lights on.
Oliver Trevelyan, Edmund Leigh, Daniel Rosen — thank you.
This has been Bleak House Unpacked.
We'll be back.

c42:p0.text:
From the verdant undulations and the spreading oaks of the Dedlock
property, Mr. Tulkinghorn transfers himself to the stale heat and
dust of London. His manner of coming and going between the two places
is one of his impenetrabilities. He walks into Chesney Wold as if it
were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he
had never been out of Lincoln’s Inn Fields. He neither changes his
dress before the journey nor talks of it afterwards. He melted out of
his turret-room this morning, just as now, in the late twilight, he
melts into his own square.
c42:p0.summary: Mr. Tulkinghorn returns from the Dedlock estate to his London chambers with characteristic mystery and detachment, indifferent to the journey and unchanged by it.
c42:p0.best_quote: He walks into Chesney Wold as if it were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he had never been out of Lincoln's Inn Fields.

c28:p37.text:
Sir Leicester is content enough that the ironmaster should feel that
there is no hurry there; there, in that ancient house, rooted in that
quiet park, where the ivy and the moss have had time to mature, and
the gnarled and warted elms and the umbrageous oaks stand deep in the
fern and leaves of a hundred years; and where the sun-dial on the
terrace has dumbly recorded for centuries that time which was as much
the property of every Dedlock—while he lasted—as the house and
lands. Sir Leicester sits down in an easy-chair, opposing his repose
and that of Chesney Wold to the restless flights of ironmasters.
c28:p37.summary: Sir Leicester finds comfort in Chesney Wold's timelessness and repose, opposing it to the restless commercial flights of modern ironmasters.
c28:p37.best_quote: where the ivy and the moss have had time to mature, and the gnarled and warted elms and the umbrageous oaks stand deep in the fern and leaves of a hundred years

c29:p3.text:
Sir Leicester sits in my Lady’s room—that room in which Mr.
Tulkinghorn read the affidavit in Jarndyce and Jarndyce—particularly
complacent. My Lady, as on that day, sits before the fire with her
screen in her hand. Sir Leicester is particularly complacent because
he has found in his newspaper some congenial remarks bearing directly
on the floodgates and the framework of society. They apply so happily
to the late case that Sir Leicester has come from the library to my
Lady’s room expressly to read them aloud. “The man who wrote this
article,” he observes by way of preface, nodding at the fire as if he
were nodding down at the man from a mount, “has a well-balanced
mind.”
c29:p3.summary: Sir Leicester reads aloud from a newspaper article to Lady Dedlock about social matters, praising the author's balanced mind.

c39:p58.text:
Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus’ purse
of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop.
Regularly, every morning at eight, is the elder Mr. Smallweed brought
down to the corner and carried in, accompanied by Mrs. Smallweed,
Judy, and Bart; and regularly, all day, do they all remain there
until nine at night, solaced by gipsy dinners, not abundant in
quantity, from the cook’s shop, rummaging and searching, digging,
delving, and diving among the treasures of the late lamented. What
those treasures are they keep so secret that the court is maddened.
In its delirium it imagines guineas pouring out of tea-pots,
crown-pieces overflowing punch-bowls, old chairs and mattresses
stuffed with Bank of England notes. It possesses itself of the
sixpenny history (with highly coloured folding frontispiece) of Mr.
Daniel Dancer and his sister, and also of Mr. Elwes, of Suffolk, and
transfers all the facts from those authentic narratives to Mr. Krook.
Twice when the dustman is called in to carry off a cartload of old
paper, ashes, and broken bottles, the whole court assembles and pries
into the baskets as they come forth. Many times the two gentlemen who
write with the ravenous little pens on the tissue-paper are seen
prowling in the neighbourhood—shy of each other, their late
partnership being dissolved. The Sol skilfully carries a vein of the
prevailing interest through the Harmonic nights. Little Swills, in
what are professionally known as “patter” allusions to the subject,
is received with loud applause; and the same vocalist “gags” in the
regular business like a man inspired. Even Miss M. Melvilleson, in
the revived Caledonian melody of “We’re a-Nodding,” points the
sentiment that “the dogs love broo” (whatever the nature of that
refreshment may be) with such archness and such a turn of the head
towards next door that she is immediately understood to mean Mr.
Smallweed loves to find money, and is nightly honoured with a double
encore. For all this, the court discovers nothing; and as Mrs. Piper
and Mrs. Perkins now communicate to the late lodger whose appearance
is the signal for a general rally, it is in one continual ferment to
discover everything, and more.
c39:p58.summary: The entire court becomes obsessed with Smallweed's search through Krook's possessions, inventing elaborate fantasies about hidden treasure. The narrator describes daily routines and even entertainment at the local pub incorporating references to the search.
c39:p58.best_quote: Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus' purse of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop.

c17:p0.text:
Richard very often came to see us while we remained in London (though
he soon failed in his letter-writing), and with his quick abilities,
his good spirits, his good temper, his gaiety and freshness, was
always delightful. But though I liked him more and more the better I
knew him, I still felt more and more how much it was to be regretted
that he had been educated in no habits of application and
concentration. The system which had addressed him in exactly the same
manner as it had addressed hundreds of other boys, all varying in
character and capacity, had enabled him to dash through his tasks,
always with fair credit and often with distinction, but in a fitful,
dazzling way that had confirmed his reliance on those very qualities
in himself which it had been most desirable to direct and train. They
were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously
won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were
very bad masters. If they had been under Richard’s direction, they
would have been his friends; but Richard being under their direction,
they became his enemies.
c17:p0.summary: Esther reflects on Richard's natural talents being undermined by his lack of discipline, a problem rooted in an educational system that addresses all students identically rather than according to individual capacity.
c17:p0.best_quote: They were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters.

c24:p20.text:
“Ada, my dear,” said Mr. Jarndyce, recovering his cheerfulness,
“these are strong words of advice, but I live in Bleak House and have
seen a sight here. Enough of that. All Richard had to start him in
the race of life is ventured. I recommend to him and you, for his
sake and your own, that he should depart from us with the
understanding that there is no sort of contract between you. I must
go further. I will be plain with you both. You were to confide freely
in me, and I will confide freely in you. I ask you wholly to
relinquish, for the present, any tie but your relationship.”
c24:p20.summary: Jarndyce proposes that Ada and Richard dissolve their romantic engagement and remain only cousins, citing his experience at Bleak House as justification.
c24:p20.best_quote: I ask you wholly to relinquish, for the present, any tie but your relationship.

c37:p115.text:
“Do you think so!” returned Mr. Skimpole. “Don’t say that, don’t say
that. Let us suppose him keeping company with Common Sense—an
excellent man—a good deal wrinkled—dreadfully practical—change for
a ten-pound note in every pocket—ruled account-book in his
hand—say, upon the whole, resembling a tax-gatherer. Our dear
Richard, sanguine, ardent, overleaping obstacles, bursting with
poetry like a young bud, says to this highly respectable companion,
‘I see a golden prospect before me; it’s very bright, it’s very
beautiful, it’s very joyous; here I go, bounding over the landscape
to come at it!’ The respectable companion instantly knocks him down
with the ruled account-book; tells him in a literal, prosaic way that
he sees no such thing; shows him it’s nothing but fees, fraud,
horsehair wigs, and black gowns. Now you know that’s a painful
change—sensible in the last degree, I have no doubt, but
disagreeable. I can’t do it. I haven’t got the ruled account-book, I
have none of the tax-gathering elements in my composition, I am not
at all respectable, and I don’t want to be. Odd perhaps, but so it
is!”
c37:p115.summary: Vholes admits Richard's attendance will not help, yet offers no objection.

c10:p9.text:
Like as he is to look at, so is his apartment in the dusk of the
present afternoon. Rusty, out of date, withdrawing from attention,
able to afford it. Heavy, broad-backed, old-fashioned,
mahogany-and-horsehair chairs, not easily lifted; obsolete tables
with spindle-legs and dusty baize covers; presentation prints of the
holders of great titles in the last generation or the last but one,
environ him. A thick and dingy Turkey-carpet muffles the floor where
he sits, attended by two candles in old-fashioned silver candlesticks
that give a very insufficient light to his large room. The titles on
the backs of his books have retired into the binding; everything that
can have a lock has got one; no key is visible. Very few loose papers
are about. He has some manuscript near him, but is not referring to
it. With the round top of an inkstand and two broken bits of
sealing-wax he is silently and slowly working out whatever train of
indecision is in his mind. Now the inkstand top is in the middle, now
the red bit of sealing-wax, now the black bit. That’s not it. Mr.
Tulkinghorn must gather them all up and begin again.
c10:p9.summary: Tulkinghorn's apartment is decorated with old-fashioned, heavy furniture, locked boxes, and dim candlelight; he sits working through some mental decision using sealing-wax and inkstand tops.
c10:p9.best_quote: everything that can have a lock has got one; no key is visible

c54:p1.text:
Thoughtful Mr. Bucket is, as a man may be with weighty work to do,
but composed, sure, confident. From the expression of his face he
might be a famous whist-player for a large stake—say a hundred
guineas certain—with the game in his hand, but with a high
reputation involved in his playing his hand out to the last card in a
masterly way. Not in the least anxious or disturbed is Mr. Bucket
when Sir Leicester appears, but he eyes the baronet aside as he comes
slowly to his easy-chair with that observant gravity of yesterday in
which there might have been yesterday, but for the audacity of the
idea, a touch of compassion.
c54:p1.summary: Bucket is thoughtful but composed, like a skilled gambler with everything at stake, regarding Sir Leicester with observant gravity and possible compassion.
c54:p1.best_quote: From the expression of his face he might be a famous whist-player for a large stake—say a hundred guineas certain—with the game in his hand, but with a high reputation involved in his playing his hand out to the last card in a masterly way.

c54:p79.text:
While this exordium is in hand—and it takes some time—Mr. Bucket,
who has seen through the transparency of Mrs. Snagsby’s vinegar at a
glance, confers with his familiar demon and bestows his shrewd
attention on the Chadbands and Mr. Smallweed. Sir Leicester Dedlock
remains immovable, with the same icy surface upon him, except that he
once or twice looks towards Mr. Bucket, as relying on that officer
alone of all mankind.
c54:p79.summary: Bucket dismisses Mrs. Snagsby's testimony while the others sit listening, and Sir Leicester shows his dependence on Bucket.
c54:p79.best_quote: Sir Leicester Dedlock remains immovable, with the same icy surface upon him, except that he once or twice looks towards Mr. Bucket, as relying on that officer alone of all mankind.

c2:p12.text:
Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.
c2:p12.summary: Despite believing herself inscrutable, Lady Dedlock is perfectly understood and managed by tradespeople and servants who deliberately lead her and her circle by flattery and careful study of her preferences.
c2:p12.best_quote: who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput

c12:p36.text:
That evening, in the housekeeper’s room, Rosa can do nothing but
murmur Lady Dedlock’s praises. She is so affable, so graceful, so
beautiful, so elegant; has such a sweet voice and such a thrilling
touch that Rosa can feel it yet! Mrs. Rouncewell confirms all this,
not without personal pride, reserving only the one point of
affability. Mrs. Rouncewell is not quite sure as to that. Heaven
forbid that she should say a syllable in dispraise of any member of
that excellent family, above all, of my Lady, whom the whole world
admires; but if my Lady would only be “a little more free,” not quite
so cold and distant, Mrs. Rouncewell thinks she would be more
affable.
c12:p36.summary: That evening, Rosa praises Lady Dedlock effusively; Mrs. Rouncewell confirms most of this but privately feels Lady Dedlock could be warmer and more affable.
c12:p36.best_quote: Mrs. Rouncewell is not quite sure as to that...Mrs. Rouncewell thinks she would be more affable.

c39:p87.text:
“A virtue in which few Englishmen are deficient,” observes Mr.
Tulkinghorn. He has been standing on the hearthstone with his back to
the smoked chimney-piece, and now turns round with his glasses to his
eyes. “Who is this? ‘Lady Dedlock.’ Ha! A very good likeness in its
way, but it wants force of character. Good day to you, gentlemen;
good day!”
c39:p87.summary: Tulkinghorn examines Lady Dedlock's portrait, comments cryptically on its weakness of character, and then takes his leave with a polite farewell.
c39:p87.best_quote: Who is this? 'Lady Dedlock.' Ha! A very good likeness in its way, but it wants force of character.

c12:p67.text:
At length, one afternoon a little before sunset, when the bright
groups of figures which have for the last hour or two enlivened the
Ghost’s Walk are all dispersed and only Sir Leicester and my Lady
remain upon the terrace, Mr. Tulkinghorn appears. He comes towards
them at his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never
slackened. He wears his usual expressionless mask—if it be a
mask—and carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every
crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great
or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his
personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients;
he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.
c12:p67.summary: At sunset, Tulkinghorn finally appears, moving at his usual methodical pace with an expressionless mask, embodying mystery and unknown knowledge.
c12:p67.best_quote: He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.

c7:p7.text:
The present representative of the Dedlocks is an excellent master. He
supposes all his dependents to be utterly bereft of individual
characters, intentions, or opinions, and is persuaded that he was
born to supersede the necessity of their having any. If he were to
make a discovery to the contrary, he would be simply stunned—would
never recover himself, most likely, except to gasp and die. But he is
an excellent master still, holding it a part of his state to be so.
He has a great liking for Mrs. Rouncewell; he says she is a most
respectable, creditable woman. He always shakes hands with her when
he comes down to Chesney Wold and when he goes away; and if he were
very ill, or if he were knocked down by accident, or run over, or
placed in any situation expressive of a Dedlock at a disadvantage, he
would say if he could speak, “Leave me, and send Mrs. Rouncewell
here!” feeling his dignity, at such a pass, safer with her than with
anybody else.
c7:p7.summary: Sir Leicester is an excellent but blind master who denies his servants any individuality, yet ironically trusts and respects Mrs. Rouncewell above all others in distress.
c7:p7.best_quote: he supposes all his dependents to be utterly bereft of individual characters, intentions, or opinions

c47:p105.text:
Phil Squod, with his smoky gunpowder visage, at once acts as nurse
and works as armourer at his little table in a corner, often looking
round and saying with a nod of his green-baize cap and an encouraging
elevation of his one eyebrow, “Hold up, my boy! Hold up!” There, too,
is Mr. Jarndyce many a time, and Allan Woodcourt almost always, both
thinking, much, how strangely fate has entangled this rough outcast
in the web of very different lives. There, too, the trooper is a
frequent visitor, filling the doorway with his athletic figure and,
from his superfluity of life and strength, seeming to shed down
temporary vigour upon Jo, who never fails to speak more robustly in
answer to his cheerful words.
c47:p105.summary: Phil Squod nurses Jo while working as an armourer; Mr. Jarndyce and Allan visit frequently; General George visits often, and all reflect on how Jo became connected to their lives.
c47:p105.best_quote: how strangely fate has entangled this rough outcast in the web of very different lives

c39:p4.text:
But not perceiving this quite plainly—only seeing it by halves in a
confused way—the laity sometimes suffer in peace and pocket, with a
bad grace, and DO grumble very much. Then this respectability of Mr.
Vholes is brought into powerful play against them. “Repeal this
statute, my good sir?” says Mr. Kenge to a smarting client. “Repeal
it, my dear sir? Never, with my consent. Alter this law, sir, and
what will be the effect of your rash proceeding on a class of
practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by
the opposite attorney in the case, Mr. Vholes? Sir, that class of
practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth. Now you
cannot afford—I will say, the social system cannot afford—to lose
an order of men like Mr. Vholes. Diligent, persevering, steady, acute
in business. My dear sir, I understand your present feelings against
the existing state of things, which I grant to be a little hard in
your case; but I can never raise my voice for the demolition of a
class of men like Mr. Vholes.” The respectability of Mr. Vholes has
even been cited with crushing effect before Parliamentary committees,
as in the following blue minutes of a distinguished attorney’s
evidence. “Question (number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight
hundred and sixty-nine): If I understand you, these forms of practice
indisputably occasion delay? Answer: Yes, some delay. Question: And
great expense? Answer: Most assuredly they cannot be gone through for
nothing. Question: And unspeakable vexation? Answer: I am not
prepared to say that. They have never given ME any vexation; quite
the contrary. Question: But you think that their abolition would
damage a class of practitioners? Answer: I have no doubt of it.
Question: Can you instance any type of that class? Answer: Yes. I
would unhesitatingly mention Mr. Vholes. He would be ruined.
Question: Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a respectable
man? Answer:”—which proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years—“Mr.
Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man.”
c39:p4.summary: Mr. Kenge's rhetorical defense of legal practitioners like Vholes is presented, along with a mock parliamentary inquiry that demonstrates how institutional self-interest defeats reform through the invocation of Vholes's respectable reputation.
c39:p4.best_quote: Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth.

c31:p92.text:
He was extremely gay all the rest of the evening, for he absolutely
chirped—those were his delighted words—when he thought by what a
happy talent for business he was surrounded. He gave us, in his glass
of negus, “Better health to our young friend!” and supposed and gaily
pursued the case of his being reserved like Whittington to become
Lord Mayor of London. In that event, no doubt, he would establish the
Jarndyce Institution and the Summerson Almshouses, and a little
annual Corporation Pilgrimage to St. Albans. He had no doubt, he
said, that our young friend was an excellent boy in his way, but his
way was not the Harold Skimpole way; what Harold Skimpole was, Harold
Skimpole had found himself, to his considerable surprise, when he
first made his own acquaintance; he had accepted himself with all his
failings and had thought it sound philosophy to make the best of the
bargain; and he hoped we would do the same.
c31:p92.summary: Skimpole cheerfully pursues fanciful thoughts about Jo becoming Lord Mayor, then expounds his philosophy of self-acceptance without moral growth.
